title: A Simple, Nearly-Optimal Algorithm for Differentially Private All-Pairs Shortest Distances

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof concludes E[X_i] > (t/2)·|A_i^r| by asserting "the last inequality follows from |A_i^r|·t ≤ n". With t = ⌈100·n^{1/k} log n⌉ and |A_1^r| = n^{1-2/k}, we get |A_1^r|·t ≈ 100·n^{1-1/k} log n, which exceeds n whenever n^{1/k} < 100 log n — i.e. for most of the admitted range k ∈ {2,…,⌊log n/log 2⌋}. Worse, the conclusion itself becomes impossible: for k = ⌊log n/log 2⌋ the lemma asserts |A_1| ≥ (t/4)·n^{1-2/k} = 25·n^{1-1/k} log n ≈ 12.5·n·log n > n, while |A_1| ≤ n. Hence Lemma 4.4 (and Lemma 4.5, which conditions on it) is false in the parameter range used by Theorems 4.3 and 4.4.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 4.3, inequality (3) (and the analogous step in Appendix D for Theorem 4.4)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Each tree is released with the ε/(t·k)-DP algorithm, where t·k = 100·k·n^{1/k}·log n, so Corollary 4.1 gives per-tree error O(t·k·log^{1.5}(n)·log(n·t·k/γ)/ε) = O(k·n^{1/k}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(n·t·k/γ)/ε). The paper instead writes O(k·n^{1/k}·log^{1.5}(n)·log(n·t·k/γ)/ε), dropping the log n coming from t, and therefore states a final bound of log^{2.5}(n) where the computation yields log^{3.5}(n). The same omission appears in Theorem 4.4 (stated log^{2.5}(n) instead of log^{3}(n)). Note that the analogous calculation in Theorems 4.1/4.2 (where the number of trees is k·n^{1/k} with no log n) is done correctly, confirming the slip.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3, paragraph introducing the input-perturbation algorithm / Lemma 3.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims the method "is a simple application of the Laplace mechanism (Lemma 2.3) to the function f : w → ℝ^{n²} which takes as input the edge weights of a graph and outputs all-pairs shortest distances" and then argues Δ₁ = 1 because "a shortest path cannot traverse any single edge more than once". The ℓ₁ sensitivity of the n²-dimensional APSD vector is Θ(n²) (each of the n² coordinates can change by up to 1), not 1; privacy here actually follows from perturbing the 1-sensitive weight vector w and post-processing. As written the sensitivity/privacy argument is invalid.

The additive error is stated as O(k·n^{1/k}·log^{2.5}(n)·log(k)·log(1/γ)/ε) "For γ ∈ (0,0.5], k ∈ ℤ⁺". For k = 1 (allowed by k ∈ ℤ⁺) the factor log(k) = 0, so the stated bound is identically 0, which is obviously false (with k = 1 the construction uses n trees and the error is Ω(n)). The simplification log(nk/γ) = O(log n·log k·log(1/γ)) (Prop. E.2) requires k ≥ 2.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 3.1 proof ("we do not release any shortest path trees themselves") and Section 4 (Corollary 4.1 applied to tree-padding spanner / TZ clusters)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Corollary 4.1 / Lemma 3.2 give an ε-DP guarantee for a FIXED tree whose topology is public (the hierarchical centroid decomposition and the 1-sensitivity argument presuppose a fixed tree). In the algorithms the trees are computed from the private edge weights (shortest-path trees from the hitting set; the Ramsey/tree-padding spanner; the clusters C^r(w) defined via true distances), so the whole mechanism's output distribution depends on private data through the tree structure. The paper's justification — "we do not release any shortest path trees themselves, hence no shortest path information is revealed" — is not a valid DP argument. Notably the paper itself reports that [CGK+23] needed the exponential mechanism to select bunches privately, which indicates that private selection of the data-dependent structure cannot simply be ignored.

"we define the bunches as B(u) = {w ∈ V | d(w,u) < d(u, p_{i+1}(u))}" contains a free index i that is never quantified, so the set is ill-defined. In Thorup–Zwick the bunch is ∪_i {w ∈ A_i \ A_{i+1} : d(w,u) < d(u, A_{i+1})}, i.e. the index is determined by the level of w. All of Lemma 4.6, the stretch analysis and Theorem 4.3 rely on this missing level condition.

The abstract says the algorithm "is the first to be optimal up to a polylogarithmic factor, based on a lower bound of Ω̃(n^{1/4})", and Section 1.1 states "we show the additive approximation problem to be Θ̃(n^{1/4})-accurate by giving a nearly optimal algorithm which matches the known lower bound". This only holds in the (ε,δ)-DP setting; the pure ε-DP result is Õ(n^{1/3}/ε), a polynomial gap from n^{1/4}. The blanket statement that the problem is Θ̃(n^{1/4})-accurate overstates the result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1 (description of [Sea16] bounded-weight results) vs Section 1.4 Related Work
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The introduction reports Sealfon's approximate-DP bounded-weight bound as Õ(√(nM/ε)), whereas the Related Work section states O(√n · M · log(1/δ)/ε · log(nMε/γ)), i.e. √n·M/ε. These two expressions are not asymptotically equivalent (√(nM/ε) vs √n·M/ε), so at least one statement of the cited result is wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Beginning of Section 4 ("a corollary of Theorem 3.2 originally proven by [Sea16]")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Corollary 4.1 is derived from Lemma 3.2 (Sealfon's rooted-tree single-source result, Theorem 4.1 in [Sea16]), as its own proof in Appendix A shows. Theorem 3.2 is this paper's (ε,δ)-DP general-graph algorithm, which is not from [Sea16] and is not what Corollary 4.1 follows from.

The step P[d(u,p_{i+1}(u)) ≤ d(u,A_i^r −{w})] ≥ 1 − (1 − 1/(2|A_i^r|))^{|A_{i+1}|} treats the |A_{i+1}| vertices as independent trials, even though A_{i+1} = ∪_r A^r_{i+1} and A^r_{i+1} ⊆ A^r_i, so the events are strongly dependent (and the bound on |A_{i+1}| from Lemma 4.4 uses the same randomness). The independence is never justified.

The displayed accuracy bound is written as |d̃^{(t)}(u,v) − d_{G̃}^{(t)}(u,v)| ≤ O(√t·log(n/γ)/ε), but the algorithm sets d̃^{(t)}(u,v) ← d_{G̃}^{(t)}(u,v), so this difference is identically zero. The quantity that must be bounded is |d̃^{(t)}(u,v) − d_G^{(t)}(u,v)| (noisy vs. true), which is the quantity in the lemma statement.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1.2 ("previous constructions [Sea16, CGK+23] also add Laplace noise ... leading to an error Õ(t/ε)")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This explanation is inconsistent with the prior bounds the paper itself reports. Under the paper's own framework (tree error Õ(s/ε), short-path error Õ(t/ε), hitting-set constraint s·t ≈ n), summing per-edge errors would give Õ(√n/ε) in the ε-DP case and Õ(n^{1/3}/ε) with advanced composition — not the Õ(n^{2/3}/ε) and Õ(√n/ε) attributed to [FLL22, CGK+23]. The stated reason for the gap therefore mischaracterizes the prior analyses.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1.4 ("In 2009, Hay et al. [HLMJ09] were the first to study differentially private graph algorithms")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Private graph analysis predates Hay et al. (2009); e.g. Nissim, Raskhodnikova and Smith (STOC 2007) already gave differentially private algorithms for graph statistics (triangle counting, MST cost). The 'first' claim is inaccurate; Hay et al. are best credited with the node/edge-DP distinction and degree-distribution estimation.

The Ramsey/tree-padding spanner construction of Abraham et al. yields a collection of trees of size O(k·n^{1/k}·log n) (an extra logarithmic covering factor is required to cover all vertices, since a single tree only handles a subset of size n^{1-1/k}). Stating the collection size as exactly k·n^{1/k} appears to drop this factor, which propagates into the explicit polylog factors of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix D, proof of Theorem 4.4 ("The stretch analysis is the same as in Theorem E.2")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: There is no Theorem E.2 (Appendix E contains Propositions E.1 and E.2 about logarithms); the intended reference is the stretch analysis of Theorem 4.3 / the (2k−1)-stretch lemma.
